newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian rebels blow up power pylon, militant dies.
newsitem.headline: Algerian rebels blow up power pylon, militant dies.

text.p: Algerian rebels blew up a power pylon and a domestic gas line in Algeria's coastal town of Cap Djinet, cutting power and gas supplies to the area, an Algerian newspaper said on Wednesday.
In a separate incident, security forces on Tuesday ambushed two Moslem guerrillas in the area, killing one of them, said the French-language Liberte newspaper.
Security forces recovered an automatic pistol on the body. The paper said the rebel's associate, named as Houas Tahar, who was sought for several deadly attacks, fled.
The newspaper said crew from state-run gas and electricity Sonelgaz company were rushed to fix the gas line and pylon damaged by two bombs detonated by guerrillas on Monday night.
There was no word on whether supplies had been restored in Cap Djinet, 40 km (25 miles) from Algiers.
The authorities blame Moslem militants for a series of bomb attacks and a sabotage campaign which caused losses to the economy of more than $2 billion.
A government-appointed human rights watchdog, National Observatory of Human Rights (ONDH), reported last month that 1,400 civilians had died in bomb attacks.

The Islamic Salvation Army (AIS), armed wing of the once powerful but now outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), this week distanced itself from more extremist guerrillas and condemned what it called "suspicious terrorist operations".

"The AIS announces to the Algerian Moslem people and to the world it rejects and condemns suspicious terrorist operations targeting unarmed innocent men, women and young people," AIS commander Madani Merzak was quoted on Wednesday as saying.
His statement appeared in the Saudi Asharq al Awsat newspaper.
Last month, Algeria's El Watan newspaper said Moslem rebels cut the throats of 17 young men after forcing them from a bus at Sidi Laadjal village, 300 km (190 miles) south of Algiers.
They killed them for refusing to join the rebel ranks, the paper said.
Merzak was quoted by Asharq al Awsat as urging guerrillas to unite under his command and purge their ranks of what he called "unruly" members.
The AIS, seen as relatively moderate, is a rival for influence among Algeria's 29 million people with the more radical Armed Islamic Group (GIA).
The GIA has claimed the killing of hundreds of people including journalists, intellectuals and religious workers.
An estimated 50,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which the banned FIS took a huge lead.
